title: Formative Assessment and School Improvement
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart applies Dylan Wiliam's classroom formative assessment framework directly to school improvement leadership, opening with a memorable Rob Coe observation that teachers use six distinct strategies to help children learn difficult things while leaders typically use just one, telling them what to do. His central argument is that just as high-stakes summative judgements of student learning contribute little to actual achievement compared to ongoing formative assessment, high-stakes judgements of teachers and schools (lesson observations used evaluatively, mock inspections, Ofsted-style reviews) likely contribute just as little to genuine school improvement. He argues the common practice of running evaluative activities like learning walks and book scrutinies and only afterward trying to make them 'formative' gets the sequence backwards, and instead proposes adapting Harry Fletcher-Wood's three components of responsive teaching, being cognizant of, sensitive to, and behaviorally supportive toward, students, into a description of what responsive school leadership toward colleagues should look like. He closes with a condensed three-part model for school improvement leadership: clarity of direction, ongoing knowledge-building about how well colleagues understand and are moving toward that direction, and adaptive support to remove barriers, explicitly rejecting summative judgement as a driver of improvement.
points: The Rob Coe 'two slides' anecdote, six strategies teachers use for student learning versus one strategy ('explain what they should do') that leaders typically use for adult learning, functions as the piece's diagnostic hook for why school improvement efforts often underperform.

Hart's central transposition argues that high-stakes evaluative judgements of teachers and schools (lesson observations, Ofsted-style reviews) likely contribute as little to genuine improvement as high-stakes summative testing contributes to student achievement, compared with ongoing formative processes.

He identifies a specific sequencing error common in school improvement: running evaluative activities (learning walks, book scrutinies) first and only afterward trying to retrofit them as 'formative,' which he argues misses the point entirely.

By substituting 'colleagues' for 'students' in Fletcher-Wood's cognizant/sensitive/behaviorally-supportive model of responsive teaching, Hart builds a directly transferable framework for what responsive, non-judgemental instructional leadership should look like day to day.

His closing three-part model (clarity of direction, ongoing knowledge-building about colleague understanding, and adaptive barrier-removing support) explicitly positions 'avoiding judgements' as a structural requirement of the model, not an optional courtesy.
quotes: The second slide was brilliantly empty. It listed the things leaders might typically do to get teachers to learn difficult things: Explain what they should do.

As Wiliam says, attending to classroom formative assessment makes more difference to student achievement than anything else. Certainly more than high stakes assessment. A similar relationship exists between our school improvement efforts and high stakes judgements of our school.
Choosing to do lesson observations, learning walks or book scrutinies and then working on making them formative misses the point. It is an example of data driven decision making.
Swapping out the word 'students' for 'colleagues' turns this into a neat description of what leaders should know and be able to do in their day to day work of tackling the problems that they face.
If colleagues need to improve something, the onus is on leaders to provide the right support rather than mandate changes and leaving colleagues to it.

Clarity of goal / direction around the problem that we are seeking to solve. Build knowledge of the extent to which colleagues understand that direction and are moving towards it. Make adjustments to the support we provide to colleagues to clarify their understanding and remove barriers to better understanding. And avoid judgements. They don't help.
